topic: Explain how rain forms, for 8 year olds

slides.body: The sun starts it, but the sky does something surprising to make water fall.

v2.evidence:
[F1] The most common failure mode in system design interviews is memorization, so spend your time learning to compose building blocks rather than recalling reference designs.
[F2] Interviewers in 2026 separate candidates on cost, failure modes, and operational judgment that used to be optional.
[F3] A 2-week system design prep plan compresses weeks 1-2 from an eight-week plan into three days of intensive fundamentals study.
[F4] In a 2-week plan, spend the remaining time after fundamentals on practice questions and at least two mock interviews.
[F5] Discussing cost trade-offs (when to use spot instances, when to cache versus recompute, when serverless makes sense) separates you from candidates who memorize architectures.
[F6] Interviewers want to see designs that feel operationally credible and product-aware, including cost, resilience, observability, and real behavior under imperfect conditions.
[F7] The most common system design interview questions in 2026 fall into seven categories: AI and LLM infrastructure, classic distributed systems, social and real-time systems, media and content delivery, data pipelines, commerce and transaction
[F8] Practice 1,300 real system design interview questions from Meta, OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and Google covering API design, data modelling, caching, sharding, replication, queues, rate limiting, consistency, and failure handling.
[F9] Start with ByteByteGo if you want the best all-around experience for system design interview prep.
[F10] Use Codemia.io or Bugfree.ai for structured and live interview practice.
[F11] Use Exponent for mock interviews with peers (free) and experts (paid).
[F12] A well-structured, clearly communicated design beats a technically superior but confusing one.

judge.notes: The deck is strong overall but could improve the hook by making the cover slide more compelling (e.g., a specific outcome or urgency). The flow is logical but the transition from slide 3 to slide 4 feels slightly abrupt; adding a brief bridge slide or adjusting the preHeader could smooth it.

slots.headline: Why using all your brain would cause a seizure
slots.body: The 10% myth sounds fun, but full activation isn't a superpower—it's a medical emergency.

slots.headline: Brain scans reveal full activity

slots.splitRight: Fact: Using all of your brain at once would cause an epileptic seizure — not superpowers.

listItems: Self-help movement: The concept gained currency in the 1920s.
World Almanac: The 1929 edition stated we use only 10%.
Pop culture: Blockbusters like 'Lucy' helped perpetuate the myth.

slides.headline: You're already using your full brain
slides.body: fMRI studies show that almost all of the brain is active most of the time.

slots.headline: You're already using your full brain
slots.body: fMRI studies show that almost all of the brain is active most of the time.

extra.hook: Why using all your brain would cause a seizure

v2.evidence:
[F1] The myth that we only use 10% of our brain is false; neuroscience shows we use virtually all parts of our brain constantly.
[F2] Modern imaging techniques like fMRI and PET confirm brain activity across all regions, even during simple tasks.
[F3] Using all of one's brain would not be desirable; such unfettered activity would almost certainly trigger an epileptic seizure.
[F4] Even at rest, a person likely uses as much of their brain as reasonably possible through the default mode network.
[F5] The 10% myth likely originated from misinterpretations of early 20th-century research by psychologists William James and Boris Sidis.
[F6] William James wrote in 1908: 'We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.'
[F7] The concept gained currency by circulating within the self-help movement of the 1920s.
[F8] The 1929 World Almanac states: 'There is NO LIMIT to what the human brain can accomplish. Scientists and psychologists tell us we use only about TEN PERCENT of our brain power.'
[F9] Blockbusters like 'Lucy', popular culture and sci-fi books helped to perpetuate the 10% brain myth.
[F10] fMRI studies show that almost all of the brain is active most of the time, debunking the myth.
[F11] Around 25 percent of the body's cholesterol is contained within the brain cells.
[F12] The 10% myth was also debunked in a study published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.

judge.notes: The cover slide is strong but could be more intriguing to drive swipes; the flow is logical and ends well, but the split slide (3) repeats the seizure point from the hero, causing slight redundancy.

v2.evidence:
[F1] In 2022, 61 UK companies took part in a six-month four-day week pilot run by 4 Day Week Global with researchers from Cambridge and Boston College.
[F2] Around 2,900 employees moved to a 32-hour week with no loss of pay.
[F3] At the end, 56 of the 61 companies said they would continue with the four-day week, and 18 made it permanent.
[F4] Revenue stayed broadly the same over the trial period, rising 1.4% on average across the companies that shared data.
[F5] Compared with the same period a year earlier, revenue grew 35%.
[F6] The number of staff leaving fell by 57%.
[F7] Sick days dropped by about two-thirds.
[F8] 39% of employees said they were less stressed, and 71% reported lower levels of burnout by the end of the trial.
[F9] Companies used different models: some gave everyone Fridays off, others staggered days, and a few used an annualised 32-hour average.
[F10] The organisers said the biggest predictor of success was cutting low-value meetings and redesigning processes before the trial started.
[F11] Critics note that participating companies volunteered, so they were likely better suited to the change than average, and that the trial was short.
[F12] Several firms in customer-facing sectors struggled with coverage and needed rota changes midway.

judge.notes: The cover slide could be stronger to immediately hook managers/HR leaders; consider leading with a business-relevant stat like '56 of 61 companies kept the four-day week' rather than sick days. The flow is logical and the deck uses real numbers accurately, including caveats. The ending is slightly abrupt; a stronger call to action or next step for the audience would improve closure.

v2.evidence:
[F1] In 2026, 70% of university students reported insufficient sleep.

[F3] 60% of university students experienced daytime sleepiness in 2026.
[F4] Insomnia prevalence among college students was 26.4% in a 2026 study.
[F5] 74.3% of college students were poor sleepers based on standardized sleep quality indices in a 2025 study.
[F6] 25.4% of college students reported binge drinking within the last 30 days.
[F7] 15.6% of students who drank alcohol used it as a sleeping aid.
[F8] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends adults sleep 7 or more hours per night.
[F9] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends teenagers 13-18 years sleep 8-10 hours per night.
[F10] Students with depression had 9.54 times higher odds of insomnia.
[F11] Students with ADHD had 3.48 times higher odds of insomnia.
[F12] Employed students had 2.10 times higher odds of insomnia.

factCheckFindings: Slide 1 (body): "Open plans cost developers 35% fewer commits daily." distorts the facts (FACTS say remote developers produce 35% more commits, not that open plans cost 35% fewer.) → Remote developers produce 35% more code commits daily than those in open-plan offices.

Slide 3 (splitLeft): "Office: Developers produce 35% fewer daily code commits due to interruptions." distorts the facts (FACTS say remote workers produce 35% more commits; the slide reverses the direction.) → Office: Developers produce 35% fewer daily code commits than remote peers due to interruptions.

Slide 5 (listItems): "Meetings doubled in two years: remote coordination compresses deep work time." is not in the facts (FACTS say meetings have doubled in two years due to remote coordination needs, but the slide omits the source and context.) → Meetings have doubled in two years due to remote coordination needs, compressing deep work time.

extra.hook: Why your office is sabotaging focus

v2.evidence:
[F1] A Stanford study of 249 call center employees found a 13% performance increase among remote workers, with gains from fewer breaks, lower attrition, and more focused time.
[F2] Remote workers average 3 hours 36 minutes of deep focus per 8-hour day, a 29% improvement over the 2 hours 48 minutes for office workers (RescueTime, 2025).
[F3] Software developers working remotely produce 35% more code commits per day than those in open-plan offices, driven by fewer interruptions (GitHub analysis of 100,000+ developers, 2024).
[F4] The average knowledge worker now gets only 2–3 hours of deep work per day, and only 39% of tracked work time is spent in genuine focus (Hubstaff 2026 Global Trends).
[F5] Meetings have doubled in two years due to remote coordination needs, directly compressing deep work time (Hubstaff 2026 benchmarks).
[F6] Cutting meetings by 40% has been shown to raise employee productivity by 71% (Flex).
[F7] A BLS study across 61 industries found a positive link between remote work and total factor productivity growth, with no drag on economic output.
[F8] A Stanford study in Nature found hybrid work has zero negative impact on performance and reduces employee turnover by 33%.
[F9] 77% of remote employees self-report higher productivity when working remotely (CoSo Cloud survey).
[F10] High-performing employees are 16% more likely to have low intent to stay if facing a return-to-office mandate (Gartner).
[F11] 67% of return-to-office mandates result in increased voluntary turnover within 6 months (Gartner HR Research).
[F12] 88% of remote workers and 79% of in-office workers report feeling pressure to appear busy, suggesting performative attendance is widespread.

judge.notes: The deck makes a clear, nuanced argument and uses evidence well. The biggest problems: (1) The cover slide's body uses a specific stat (35% more code commits) that, while compelling, may not hook all knowledge workers/managers as effectively as a broader, more relatable claim about deep work. (2) Slide 5's list item 'Cutting meetings by 40% can raise productivity by 71%' is sourced from Flex, but the deck doesn't clarify that this is a separate study, not directly about remote work, which could confuse the flow.

topic: A 12 slide deep dive on how transformer models work

slides.headline: What is a parameter anyway?
slides.body: It's a learned number inside a transformer. But how do billions of them work together to produce language? Let's explore.

slots.headline: What is a parameter anyway?
slots.body: It's a learned number inside a transformer. But how do billions of them work together to produce language? Let's explore.

slides.headline: A Parameter Is a Learned Number
slides.body: Inside a transformer, a parameter is a single learned number that forms part of large matrices called weights, plus a few biases. These numbers are the model's internal knowledge, adjusted during training to improve predictions.

slots.headline: A Parameter Is a Learned Number
slots.body: Inside a transformer, a parameter is a single learned number that forms part of large matrices called weights, plus a few biases. These numbers are the model's internal knowledge, adjusted during training to improve predictions.

slides.body: Transformer models often exceed 10 billion parameters, enabling complex pattern learning.

slots.headline: Models Often Exceed 10 Billion Parameters

slides.headline: The Feed-Forward Network Is the Largest Component
slides.body: The feed-forward network (FFN) is the largest component by parameter count in most transformers, containing roughly two-thirds of all parameters. This makes the FFN the dominant driver of model size and computational cost.

slots.headline: The Feed-Forward Network Is the Largest Component

slides.headline: Training Nudges Parameters to Improve Predictions
slides.body: Training is the process of nudging all parameters until the model predicts well. Each small adjustment moves the model closer to producing accurate outputs, ultimately shaping the knowledge stored in its weights.

slides.headline: Performance Improves Smoothly with Scale
slides.body: Researchers found that performance improved smoothly and predictably as they increased parameters, training data, and compute together. This scaling behavior is a core principle behind modern large language models.

factCheckFindings: Slide 9 (body): "Training GPT-4 cost $79 million in 2026 for 8,192-token context, covering compute until convergence." distorts the facts (FACTS state GPT-4 training cost is estimated at $79 million in 2026, but the slide incorrectly says 'in 2026' for the cost; the fact says the cost estimate is f) → Training GPT-4 cost an estimated $79 million in 2023 for an 8,192-token context, covering compute until convergence.

v2.evidence:
[F1] Transformer models typically have large parameter counts, often exceeding 10 billion.
[F2] The feed-forward network (FFN) is the largest component by parameter count in most Transformers, containing roughly 2/3 of all parameters.
[F3] A parameter is a learned number inside a transformer, part of large matrices of numbers called weights (plus a few biases).
[F4] Training is the process of nudging all parameters until the model predicts well.
[F5] Researchers found that performance improved smoothly and predictably as they increased parameters, training data, and compute together.
[F6] DeepMind's Chinchilla rule recommends training on roughly 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal performance.
[F7] Active parameter count per token is shifting from total parameters as the key metric, because it determines inference cost.
[F8] GPT-4 training cost is estimated at $79 million in 2026, with a context length of 8,192 tokens.
[F9] The cost to train a 'GPT-4 equivalent' model declined from $79M in 2023 to an estimated $5–$10M in 2026.
[F10] The attention mechanism accounts for up to 80% of the efficiency gained in text processing tasks.
[F11] Transformer models have made remarkable progress in computer vision, largely due to their ability to capture global relationships through self-attention.
[F12] The Transformer architecture has transformed various industries by enhancing natural language processing capabilities.

judge.notes: The deck is strong on clarity and accuracy, but the hook could be more compelling for developers new to ML—the cover slide's question is good but lacks a concrete, surprising angle. Also, the deck misses explicit coverage of tokens, embeddings, and next-token prediction, which are required by 'A GOOD DECK MUST'—this is a notable gap.
